title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 18: An Easter Message to Rotary
primary_topics: Chapter 18 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's Easter message printed in the Rotary Balita of April 4, 1991 while he was president of the Rotary Club of Manila, arguing that 'Easter, not Christmas, is the most glorious event in Christendom' because the resurrection proves Christ's divinity and without it 'Christianity would be meaningless'

The passion as the model of 'the Christian ethic of active non-violence' -- Christ, innocent of the mob's charge of 'blasphemy,' endured ridicule, whip-lashings, cross-carrying and death, and by rising triumphed over 'mob emotionalism, false charges, human suffering and sin'

The personal application: every Christian must pass through 'our own passion and death' -- not physical death but the renunciation of 'attachment to sin, to worldliness, to lust' -- because 'how can there be resurrection without crucifixion?'

The Rotarian application: concrete, everyday cross-carrying -- choosing spouse and children over lust, paying honest taxes where evasion is safe, refusing to exploit the weaker party, and serving 'the least of our brethren' rather than 'luxuriating in our air-conditioned offices'
sub_topics: He opens with 'HAPPY EASTER!' and an immediate thesis: Easter, not Christmas, is Christendom's most glorious event
He draws the contrast -- Christmas 'marks the birth of Jesus as a human being,' Easter 'celebrates His divinity'; Christmas is 'the joyful beginning' and Easter 'the glorious victory'
He states the stakes: by rising, Jesus 'triumphed over evil, saved man from sin and erased all doubts that, indeed, He is God,' and without the resurrection Christianity would be meaningless
He reads the passion as a demonstration of active non-violence: Christ absorbed a false charge, public ridicule and death rather than answer them in kind
He turns the feast into a personal demand -- believers 'too, must go through our own passion and death' before they can 'rise and to live a life on high with Jesus Christ'
He redefines that death as spiritual: renouncing sin and reforming one's life 'in accord with the basic Christian doctrine of love (love for God and neighbor)'

He gives Rotarians four concrete tests of cross-carrying: fidelity over self-gratification, honest taxes where evasion is undetectable, refusing to take advantage of the weaker, and hands-on service to 'the least of our brethren'
He clinches the argument with Christ's own words, 'He who will not take up his cross and come after me is not worthy of me' (Matt. 10:38)
He closes on daily practice: Easter is celebrated 'in our lives daily as we choose honesty over deceit, hard work over easy money, virtue over vice, love over vengeance'
signature_phrases: Easter, not Christmas, is the most glorious event in Christendom
Christmas is the joyful beginning but Easter is the glorious victory
For how can there be resurrection without crucifixion?

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 18 of 'Love God, Serve Man' reprints the Easter message Artemio V. Panganiban wrote for the Rotary Balita issue of April 4, 1991, while he was president of the Rotary Club of Manila. He opened with the claim that 'Easter, not Christmas, is the most glorious event in Christendom,' reasoning that Christmas 'marks the birth of Jesus as a human being' while Easter 'celebrates His divinity' -- Christmas being 'the joyful beginning' and Easter 'the glorious victory.' By His resurrection, he wrote, Jesus 'triumphed over evil, saved man from sin and erased all doubts that, indeed, He is God,' and without that resurrection 'Christianity would be meaningless.' He then read the passion as a demonstration of 'the Christian ethic of active non-violence': though innocent of the mob's charge of 'blasphemy,' Christ endured public ridicule, whip-lashings, cross-carrying and death, and in rising triumphed over 'mob emotionalism, false charges, human suffering and sin.' Turning the feast into a personal demand, he argued that believers too must pass through 'our own passion and death' before they can rise, asking 'how can there be resurrection without crucifixion?' -- and clarifying that this death need not be physical but may be the renunciation of 'attachment to sin, to worldliness, to lust,' a reform of life 'in accord with the basic Christian doctrine of love (love for God and neighbor).' He gave his fellow Rotarians four concrete tests of cross-carrying: choosing spouse and children over lust and self-gratification; paying honest taxes 'particularly where evasion has little risk of discovery'; refusing to take advantage of another despite superior talent or resources; and rolling up their sleeves to serve 'the least of our brethren' rather than 'luxuriating in our air-conditioned offices.' He quoted Christ's warning that 'He who will not take up his cross and come after me is not worthy of me' (Matt. 10:38), and closed on daily practice: Easter is celebrated 'in our lives daily as we choose honesty over deceit, hard work over easy money, virtue over vice, love over vengeance.'
